newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Britain sees 1997 as crucial for divided Cyprus.
newsitem.headline: Britain sees 1997 as crucial for divided Cyprus.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Monday that 1997 could be a make-or-break year for divided Cyprus and warned that further militarisation could scupper efforts to start peace talks between Greeks and Turks.

Rifkind, the first foreign secretary to visit the divided island for more than 30 years, outlined a 10-point proposal which he said could help the two communities overcome the legacy of hatred but acknowledged huge problems remained.

"I sense there is a view in both communities that 1997 is a crucial year which could mark radical progress or be a massive lost opportunity," he told reporters after a meeting with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

Both the internationally recognised government in the Greek Cypriot part of the Mediterranean island and the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north have beefed up defences and Rifkind said the levels of armaments were "dangerously high".

The extent of the island's problems was emphasised when Denktash accused Greek Cypriot leader Glafcos Clerides of sabotaging the prospects for the face-to-face talks which the international community wants to see early next year.
Both leaders agree in principle that the way forward was to turn Cyprus into a bicommunal federation, but neither has found it politically possible to start face-to-face talks.

Denktash also poured water on British suggestions that Cyprus's accession talks to the European Union in 1998 could be used to persuade the Greeks and Turks to strike a deal, saying the EU talks would have to wait until a political settlement had been made.
In his separate talks with Denktash and Clerides the British minister put across the message that the world wants to see an end to a conflict which is seen as a throwback to an earlier age.

In the 10 points, Rifkind said the boundaries of a future federation of Cyprus should not follow the present ceasefire line. He called on both sides to take steps to encourage mutual confidence as the parties slowly made their peace.
"One cannot reverse 30 years of disappointments in an evening, or a week, or several months," he said.

The United Nations has nothing to show for 20 years of efforts to broker a peace but British officials said the world had to make a concerted effort to prevent the increasing tension on the island from spilling over into conflict.
Turkey, Greece and Britain, the former colonial power until independence in 1960, are guarantor powers of Cyprus.

Four people have died in a series of clashes along the Green Line this year and the prospects for peace talks look uncertain, especially since the Cypriots have recently bought battle tanks and armoured personnel carriers and plan to buy ground-to-air missiles.
"If there are prospects for a solution, they cannot be assisted by further militarisation of the island. It would be a big step in the wrong direction," Rifkind told reporters.
"The amount of military hardware and personnel on Cyprus is already absurdly high and dangerously high."

The Turkish foreign ministry said the matter of possible missile sales by Moscow to the Greek Cypriot part of Cyprus would be on the agenda when Turkey's Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller travels to Russia this week.

Rifkind also toured the United Nations buffer zone which divides Nicosia where he saw bullet-ridden and smashed houses untouched since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded the northern third of the island after a Greek-sponsored coup.
